questions.q: What is the standard ratio of length:breadth:height for Harappan baked bricks, and at which major site was this ratio first systematically documented?
questions.a: The standard ratio is 4:2:1 (e.g., 28 cm × 14 cm × 7 cm), first systematically documented at Mohenjo-daro. A wrong answer (e.g., 3:2:1 or "varied by city") reveals the student memorized a fact without understanding the civilization-wide standardization that implies central regulation of production — a core concept for board-level analysis of state control.

questions.q: Why did Harappan cities consistently orient their main streets along cardinal directions (north-south, east-west) rather than following terrain?
questions.a: Cardinal orientation optimized wind circulation for ventilation, aligned drainage gradients for gravity flow, and may have reflected cosmological/astronomical knowledge. A wrong answer like "it was easier to build" or "they copied Mesopotamia" shows the student treats planning as arbitrary convenience rather than a deliberate multi-functional system integrating climate, sanitation, and possibly ritual — missing the analytical depth required for "analyze" level.

questions.q: A newly excavated Harappan site shows a citadel mound but no grid streets in the lower town — instead, lanes curve organically. Using the principle of "civic uniformity," evaluate whether this site fits the mature Harappan urban model.
questions.a: It does not fit the mature Harappan model. Mature phase (2600–1900 BCE) sites across 1.5 million sq km show mandatory grid planning; organic lanes suggest either an early/pre-urban phase (like Kot Diji) or a regional variant without central oversight. A wrong answer accepting it as "local variation" misses that uniformity is the defining diagnostic of the mature phase — a board-exam distinction between mature Harappan and earlier/local cultures.

questions.q: Compare the drainage systems of Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira. What does the difference in construction material (baked brick vs. stone) reveal about Harappan urban planning?
questions.a: Mohenjo-daro used baked bricks; Dholavira used locally quarried stone with precisely cut channels. Both achieve the same functional standard (covered, gradient-maintained, inspection manholes). This reveals planning principles were portable and adaptable to local resources — the *design logic* (gradient, coverage, access) was standardized, not just the materials. A wrong answer focusing only on material difference ("one used brick, one stone") fails to analyze the underlying uniform engineering philosophy.

questions.q: Some historians argue the "citadel" was a religious center, others a administrative elite residence. Using only urban planning evidence (layout, access, associated structures), which interpretation is better supported and why?
questions.a: Administrative elite residence is better supported. Citadels are physically separated (walled, raised), contain large non-residential structures (granaries, assembly halls), and control access to lower towns — consistent with governance. The Great Bath is the only clearly ritual structure, but it is singular per city. A wrong answer choosing "religious center" based solely on the Great Bath ignores the citadel's overall spatial dominance and secular infrastructure (granaries), showing inability to weigh multiple lines of archaeological evidence.

questions.q: Design a 5-point checklist an archaeologist would use to confirm a newly discovered site belongs to the *mature* Harappan urban phase (not early or late). Each point must be a planning feature, not an artifact type.
questions.a: 1) Citadel on raised western mound with fortification wall. 2) Lower town laid out on cardinal grid with streets ≥ 9 m wide. 3) Covered drainage with inspection chambers at regular intervals. 4) Uniform baked-brick ratio 4:2:1 in all major structures. 5) Presence of at least one large public infrastructure (Great Bath, granary, or reservoir complex). A poor answer lists artifacts (seals, pottery) or omits the grid/drainage/brick triad, showing the student cannot distinguish urban planning diagnostics from cultural material — a critical board-exam skill.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Harappan (Sindhu-Sarasvati) ______'s urban planning (c.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are visiting Dholavira in Gujarat and notice the city is divided into a high walled citadel and a lower town with streets crossing at perfect right angles, plus ______ carved into stone.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the grid layout, standardized bricks, and drainage system demonstrate centralized planning and social organization, and can compare Harappan urban features with at least one contemporary civilisation (Mesopotamia/Egypt) to identify unique indigenous innovations.
